h1: A LinkedIn profile that gets brewers noticed by recruiters
title: A LinkedIn Profile for Brewers | Craft Beer School
desc: How brewers and aspiring brewers can build a LinkedIn profile recruiters find: headline, about section, experience, skills and keywords.
teaser: Recruiters search LinkedIn for words like brewer, fermentation and packaging. If those words are not on your profile, you do not exist to them.
standfirst: Many brewery jobs in India are filled through referrals and LinkedIn searches before they are ever advertised. We show how to build a profile that recruiters and head brewers can find and that makes them want to call you.
sections:
Brewery hiring in India often happens quietly. A head brewer asks around, a recruiter searches LinkedIn for people with fermentation or packaging experience, or a founder looks for someone who has worked on a similar brewhouse. If your profile is empty or vague, you will not show up.

A good profile does not need to be fancy. It needs the right words, clear facts about what you have done and evidence that you know your craft.

Your headline is the line under your name. It appears in search results, so it matters most. Avoid "Looking for opportunities" or just your current job title. Say what you do and what you know.

Examples of the pattern:

  • "Assistant Brewer, brewpub, lagers and wheat beers, cellar and CIP"
  • "Microbiology graduate moving into brewing, yeast handling and QC lab skills"
  • "Homebrewer and food technologist, all-grain brewing, sensory training"

Use a clear, friendly photo with good light. A photo in the brewhouse in work clothes is fine and shows you belong there.

Write three short paragraphs in plain language. First, what you do now and what you are good at. Second, your brewing experience and knowledge, with specifics. Third, what kind of role you want next.

Be specific instead of using adjectives. "Passionate brewer with strong skills" says nothing. "I brew on a 5 hl brewhouse, run yeast counts and handle CIP for six fermenters" says a lot, if it is true. Never inflate your experience. Head brewers will test you in interview. Brewing is a small world.
Experience that shows what you can do

For each role, list what you actually did with brewing details:

  • Brewhouse size and type, plus what you were responsible for.
  • Styles you brewed regularly.
  • Cellar, filtration, packaging or lab tasks you handled.
  • Improvements you were part of, described honestly. For example: "Helped set up a daily gravity and temperature log for all fermenters."
  • Safety or hygiene responsibilities.

If you are moving from another field, show the transferable skills: lab work, food safety, maintenance, quality systems or sensory work. Our guide to the brewer CV and interview covers how to present the same facts on paper.

Recruiters search with keywords. Include the words that match your experience: brewing, fermentation, wort production, cellar operations, yeast management, CIP, filtration, packaging, quality control, sensory evaluation, HACCP, food safety. Use the terms people in the industry actually use.

List relevant certifications and courses, with the body and date. Add brewing courses, food safety training, safety courses and sensory training. Do not list things you have not completed.

Ask two or three people you have worked with for a short recommendation that mentions something specific, such as how you ran a brew day or handled a cleaning schedule. A line from a head brewer carries real weight with other head brewers.

Turn on the setting that shows recruiters you are open to work. LinkedIn lets you show this only to recruiters, which is useful if you are currently employed.

Profiles that show activity stand out. Post occasionally about what you are learning: a brew day, a style you studied, a lesson from a mistake. Share photos of your homebrew or brewhouse work, with permission from your employer if needed. Comment thoughtfully on posts by brewers and breweries.

If you write, keep posts short and specific. One photo of a cloudy wort run-off with two lines on what you changed says more than a long essay about passion. Keep it professional. Avoid posts that show heavy drinking. Do not share confidential recipes or details from an employer. A recruiter looking at your activity should see someone serious about brewing.

Connect with brewers, head brewers, brewery founders and recruiters who work in drinks. Add a short note explaining who you are. Join brewing groups and follow breweries you would like to work for.

Look for internships and junior roles too. Our guide to brewery internships in India explains how many brewers got their first break.

A strong profile gets you noticed. What gets you hired is the knowledge behind it: being able to talk confidently about mashing, fermentation and quality when the call comes.
faqs: What should a brewer put in their LinkedIn headline?
Your role or target role plus your key skills, such as styles, cellar work, CIP or lab skills. Avoid vague lines like "looking for opportunities".
Which keywords do brewery recruiters search for?
Terms like brewing, fermentation, cellar operations, yeast management, CIP, packaging, quality control and food safety, matched to your real experience.
Can I show I am open to work without my employer seeing?
LinkedIn lets you show your open-to-work status to recruiters only. Check the current settings to be sure.
